# Metrics

**Generated from `metrics.Catalogue()`. Do not edit — change the catalogue.**

The engine exports OpenTelemetry metrics through the same `OTEL_*` environment
its traces use, because a company has one telemetry backend and two settings
would let you split signals across two of them where a correlation resolves on
neither:

| Variable | What it does |
|---|---|
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` | The collector. Metrics are posted to `<endpoint>/v1/metrics`. |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_ENDPOINT` | Overrides the base for metrics alone. |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL` | `http/protobuf` (default) or `grpc`. |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` | Sent with every export — an API key, a tenant. |
| `OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER` | `none` switches the export off and leaves traces on. |
| `OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL` | Export period in milliseconds. Default 60000. |

**The provider is installed whether or not you are collecting.** Every
instrument exists either way, so no code path in the engine branches on
whether metrics are "on", and the numbers on `crewlet retention status` are
read from the same recorder a collector would be reading. With no endpoint set
the measurements are taken and not shipped.

**Every attribute below is a closed set.** No metric carries a task key, a
subject id, a page title or a node id as an attribute — the node is the
resource, set once — so the number of time series is bounded by this page
rather than by how much work your company has done.

## Histograms

A distribution, exported with the engine's own bucket boundaries, which are its unit's: in `ms`, 1, 2 and 5 times every power of ten from 10 µs to 5·10⁷ ms (nearly fourteen hours), so every budget an alarm holds a percentile to is a boundary and the alarm fires exactly past it; in `1`, the same series from 1 to 500 000; in `By`, every power of two from 1 KiB to 2 GiB. Each resolves a percentile to within a factor of two and a half at every scale its unit is recorded at, from a 40 µs index probe to a backup of hours and a push's bundle of a gibibyte. The SDK's default boundaries stop at 10 s, so a slow apply would land in an overflow bucket and read as "at least 10 s" for ever.

| Metric | Unit | Attributes | What it makes visible |
|---|---|---|---|
| `crewlet.statelog.publish.duration` | `ms` | `domain`, `outcome` | A write path slowing down before it starts refusing. The outcome dimension separates the three answers a write has, so a rise in `pending` reads as an applier falling behind rather than as a broker getting slower. |
| `crewlet.statelog.publish.rounds` | `1` | `domain` | Contention on one subject, which the compare-and-set round cap bounds and nothing measured. A distribution creeping toward the cap is a hot object; reaching it is a refusal a model reads as a colleague editing the same thing. |
| `crewlet.statelog.write.session_wait` | `ms` | `domain` | The wait a write pays for its own previous write to apply. Zero when the caller is caught up, which is the common case, and the shape of the load that is not. |
| `crewlet.statelog.barrier.duration` | `ms` | `domain` | The broker round trip under every linearizable read, and the first number a drifting fsync or a degrading quorum moves. It was a benchmark's p50 on an idle loopback cluster and nothing in production. |
| `crewlet.statelog.read.wait` | `ms` | `domain`, `level` | How much of the read budget a barrier or session wait actually spends. A p95 approaching the budget is reads about to start refusing, which is the warning the refusal itself is too late to be. |
| `crewlet.statelog.apply.latency` | `ms` | `domain` | THE COMMIT-TO-APPLY GAP: from the broker's own timestamp on a record to this node committing it. Every read level is a policy about this quantity and nothing measured it. |
| `crewlet.statelog.apply.tx.duration` | `ms` | `domain`, `bound_by` | How long one apply transaction holds the store's writer, and which budget ended it. A transaction is what every waiter behind it pays, and rows were only ever a proxy for the duration. |
| `crewlet.statelog.apply.record.duration` | `ms` | `domain`, `kind` | One record's apply. A single record past the time budget is still one transaction, so this is the real ceiling on how long a read can be delayed — a sentence in a design document until it was measured. |
| `crewlet.statelog.apply.batch.rows` | `1` | `domain` | Rows per apply transaction, which is what the row budget bounds and what the drain rate divides. |
| `crewlet.backup.duration` | `ms` | — | How long a backup took, which is the window the trim hold covers and the I/O the copy spends competing with the applier's own commits. It is what turns the retention guide's worked example into a number for THIS hardware. |
| `crewlet.store.pool.wait` | `ms` | `file` | How long a reader waited for a connection. It is what says the reader pool is too small on this node, which nothing could say before. |
| `crewlet.tracker.search.scan.duration` | `ms` | `path`, `rung` | One search's scan, recorded by the node that coordinated it, split by what it ran for (`path`: `prefetch` for a turn's knowledge prefetch, which the turn waits on before its first token, `interactive` for somebody's deliberate search) and by the ranking it actually served (`rung`: hybrid, keyword, semantic, or none). Each path has its own budget — half a second for a prefetch (`prefetch_slow`), a second for an interactive search (`search_slow`) — and read as one series the quicker one hides the other; a keyword scan is a fraction of a fused one's cost, so reading rungs as one series hides a slow meaning half. |
| `crewlet.objects.s3.request.attempts` | `1` | `operation`, `outcome` | How many attempts each request of this node's S3 client took, observed once as it ends, by `operation` and how it ended (`outcome`): `answered` — the bucket's final answer, a success or a refusal; `given_up` — the bucket answered nothing but failures (server errors that are no throttle, or no answer at all) from the first to a bound drawn for it between forty seconds and a minute after it, or stopped moving one of its attempts for a minute (`stalled` on the attempts counter), so the request was not asked again and its caller was told the bucket's last answer; `ended` — its deadline or its caller ended it after at least one attempt, one still throttled among them; `unsent` — it ended before its first attempt, observed at zero: its deadline or its caller ended it while it waited at the gate (the gate starving the node's requests), or it was refused before sending; `failed` — a failure asking again cannot change, such as a certificate the node does not trust, or an S3 Express session that could not be had for it. Nothing counts a request's attempts but its deadline and that bound, so the tail is how long the bucket made requests wait: a p95 above one is a bucket throttling or failing, and `given_up` above zero is a bucket that failed every attempt for most of a minute, or held one for a whole minute without moving it. |
| `crewlet.code.commit.batch.size` | `1` | — | Pushes per code record: group commit working, or not. The committer takes everything already queued behind an in-flight record — without lingering for more — so an idle repository's records stay at one push and a busy one's grow, up to 64. A busy repository whose batches stay at one is one whose pushes arrive more slowly than a record commits. |
| `crewlet.code.home.facts.duration` | `ms` | `outcome` | One revision's facts as this node's home loop asked them of the repository's git nodes — its merge base, the files it touches and its patch-id against its target's tip — by `outcome`: `answered` or `failed`. Read by the home itself unless its copy cannot answer, the runner-up then: a 1 MiB patch takes some 20 ms and one at the 256 MiB bound some 2.3 s on two cores. Durations near the read's ten seconds of git are changes past what a home identifies — their patch-ids omitted — or a home short of the CPU its reads run on. |
| `crewlet.code.compact.duration` | `ms` | `outcome` | One compaction from its plan to its answer, by `outcome` (as `crewlet.code.compact.runs` counts them): the sync, the plan, the build, every output's upload and the committer's decide. A merge of a few small packs takes under a second; one of several gigabytes, minutes of its build and of the store's pace. `applied` durations rising while the pushes hold steady are a maintaining node short of the CPU its builds run on, or of the bandwidth to its object store. |
| `crewlet.code.publish.duration` | `ms` | `outcome` | One publication from its plan to its answer, by `outcome` (as `crewlet.code.publish.runs` counts them): the sync, the plan, the repack, the layer's bitmap — a walk of the repository's whole history, seconds at a gigabyte and minutes at the largest — every part's and output's upload, and the committer's decide. Its build is what paces the repository's next publication: at most a tenth of the node's time. |
| `crewlet.code.cache.check.duration` | `ms` | `trigger` | How long one check of a copy's index files, or one scrub of every file it holds, took, by `trigger` (`first`, `unvouched`, `scrub`, `report`, `forced` or `request`, as `crewlet.code.cache.checks`), counted only where it read something. A check is what a copy's first request after a restart waited for beside its sync — about a quarter of the copy's pack bytes read; a scrub runs behind the serving and nobody waits for it, reading every byte the copy holds. Both hash on one core, a read slot a 64 MiB piece, and at the volume's own throughput when read cold. |
| `crewlet.code.cache.layer.install` | `ms` | `outcome` | How long one published layer took this node's git cache to install, from its staging to its placement — its parts' downloads, each beside the others in one of the node's fetch slots, its files' syncs and its check against its row, and the placement's bitmapped read through it — by `outcome` (`installed`, `adopted`, `missing`, `corrupt`, `failed`, as `crewlet.code.cache.layers`). A full sync fetches its layers beside its packs and a cold copy's first answer waits for them; the installer, behind the serving, keeps at most half the node's downloads for itself. A p95 climbing with `installed` steady is an object store slowing down; `failed` climbing, one failing. |
| `crewlet.code.cache.sync.duration` | `ms` | `kind` | How long a completed cache sync took, by `kind` (`delta`: the rows moved since the cache's position; `full`: the whole repository — a cold cache, the first sync of a repository after a restart, a log recreated under it), from its round's start: the read of its rows, its downloads and its writes, and for a `full` sync its wait for one of the eight full reads the node runs at once (`crewlet.code.cache.full_rounds`). A delta p95 climbing is a node falling behind its pushes. A full sync's time is mostly its downloads, sixteen at once, on a cache that never held the repository — but on a node bringing up many repositories at once, above all one restarted over the cache it kept, which downloads nothing, it is mostly that wait: `full_rounds` `waiting` climbing says so, not the object store. |
| `crewlet.code.cache.read.page.duration` | `ms` | `kind` | How long one page of a repository's rows took the estate to answer this node's cache, by `kind` (`full`: a page of a whole repository's rows — a full sync's, a check's or a hint's; `delta`: a page of what moved since the cache's position), from the ask to the answer: the data node's lane and reader connection, its scan of the page and the crossing — or, on a node that holds the data, its own store's. A full page of refs, ten thousand of them, takes about 60 ms to scan, and a repository of a few hundred refs is one page of a few milliseconds: a `full` p95 far under 60 ms is full reads holding the node's eight slots (`crewlet.code.cache.full_rounds`) briefly, and one climbing past it is a data node whose readers queue — `crewlet.store.pool.wait` there says so. It is production's reading of the page the node's eight full reads at once were measured against. |
| `crewlet.code.git.wait` | `ms` | `class` | How long a git process waited for a slot on this node, by `class` (`read`, `transfer`, `maintenance`). A p95 approaching ten seconds is a node about to answer clones and pushes with 503 — every slot of one lane busy for a whole read attempt. `transfer` waiting is a node serving as many clones and pushes as `git.max_transfers` admits (more git nodes, or more memory and a wider `git.max_transfers`); `read` waiting is a node out of `git.max_processes`, one core a slot. |
| `crewlet.code.git.cpu` | `ms` | `class` | CPU a git process tree spent, by lane: `transfer` is clones and pushes, `read` the cache's reads and a push's scans and fetch checks, `maintenance` the bitmaps, indexes and checks. One observation per process, its whole cost, recorded when it ends: its user and system time and that of every process it waited for (upload-pack's pack-objects, receive-pack's index-pack) — and for one the node ended (a deadline, a stall, a client gone) at least what its whole group had spent when it was signalled; on macOS, only what the process and the children it had reaped spent. So the sum is what a lane's runs cost, read over a window longer than the runs it counts — a clone may run for hours and a bitmap for a quarter of an hour, each landing whole in the window it ends in — and never the share of the node git is taking now, which is the container's own CPU usage. Read the sum and the count rather than the percentiles: a run past 64 s of CPU lands in the last bin. |
| `crewlet.code.git.share_wait` | `ms` | `share` | How long a clone, fetch or push waited for its transfer slot on this node, by the `share` it waited in (`person`: the holder of a human seat — a person through any credential of theirs, or a Tier A token or service account the identity directory binds to a human seat nobody else holds; `machine`: a credential acting as nobody, a Tier A token or a service account's machine token bound to no seat; `run`: a coding box's git, with its run's credential on `/box/git/`). When every slot is held a released one goes to the class furthest below its weighted share of what the lane spent lately (person 4 : machine 2 : run 1), so `machine` climbing while `person` stays flat is the share doing its job — CI waiting behind CI, not people behind CI — and `person` and `machine` both climbing is a lane too narrow for its traffic: more memory and a wider `git.max_transfers`, or more git nodes. Coding boxes together hold at most half the lane, so `run` climbing alone is boxes waiting behind each other at that bound, never a person behind a box. |
| `crewlet.code.push.duration` | `ms` | `outcome` | How long a git push took on this node, from its request to its answer, by `outcome` (`applied`, `pending`, `unknown`, `refused`, `failed`). `pending` growing is a code log whose records are durable and slow to apply here; `unknown` is a committer that stopped answering; the tail of `applied` is what a person waits for a push. |
| `crewlet.code.push.bytes` | `By` | — | The size of each push's bundle — the pack its receive-pack kept and the two indexes it wrote — observed once the pack is checked, whatever becomes of the push: the one object the object store stores for it, against `code.limits.max_push_bytes` (what the client may send) and the 1.25 GiB one push may store. |
| `crewlet.code.fetch.duration` | `ms` | `command`, `sync` | How long a fetch request took on this node, by `command` (`advertise`, `ls-refs`, `fetch`) and by what the cache had to do first (`sync`: `none`, `delta`, `full`). A `full` tail is cold caches downloading whole repositories; a `delta` tail is the barrier and the sync every answer that names a ref waits for. |
| `crewlet.code.host.spool.wait` | `ms` | `outcome` | How long each fetch counted by `crewlet.code.host.spool.waits` waited for room to spool, by the same `outcome` (`granted`, `expired`, `abandoned`; a `refused` one waited for nothing). The `granted` tail is what the wait adds to a checkout; one nearing 55 s is a node about to answer checkouts 503. |
| `crewlet.code.host.write.duration` | `ms` | `kind`, `stage` | How long each engine write took on this node, by `kind` and `stage`: `sync`, bringing the copy to the caller's floor and judging the write on it, the check of what it names among it; `build`, its git — the lookups of what it changes, its objects, its commit and its pack, under a unit of the seat git-work share; `land`, the landing every push takes — the upload, the proposal and the wait for its row; and `total`. A `build` tail near ten seconds is changes too wide for an engine write, answered too_large; a `land` tail is the code log's, as a push's is. |
| `crewlet.artifacts.publish.duration` | `ms` | `outcome` | How long one create, publish or asset finalize took through the pipeline (read back, edits, lint, CDN copies, the domain's decide), by `outcome`: `published`, `refused` (the request was judged and turned down) or `failed` (no outcome could be established, which is a store or a broker not answering). The publish latency objective is read from it. |
| `crewlet.artifacts.serve.duration` | `ms` | `dest` | How long the artifact origin took to answer, by `dest`, the whole response included. A document's tail is the time to first byte a viewer waits on before a frame can render, which the service objective for viewing reads; a slow subresource tail with fast documents is the object store. |
| `crewlet.artifacts.data.write.duration` | `ms` | `verdict` | How long a datastore write takes from the request to its verdict read back from this node's rows, by verdict (applied, conflict, invalid, forbidden, quota, gone, or pending where this node had not applied it yet, rate_limited and refused_early before anything was appended). The datastore op objective is a p95 of 250 ms; a rise in pending reads as this node's applier falling behind. |
| `crewlet.artifacts.push.lag` | `ms` | `kind` | How long after the broker stored a committed datastore batch's newest record its `artifact_data` push was handed to this node's sockets (`kind` `data`): the applier's lag plus the fan-out. A datastore change is held to reach the socket within a second. An artifacts movement carries no broker instant, so `artifact_changed` is not measured here; its lag is the artifacts applier's own, in the state log's apply instruments. |
| `crewlet.artifacts.ready.duration` | `ms` | `outcome` | How long a frame took from its view ticket being minted to the page's bridge hello, as the viewer's browser reported it through `POST /artifacts/ready`, by `outcome` (`ready`, or `failed` for a frame that never said hello). The only artifacts instrument that sees an outage keeping requests from reaching the engine at all (the artifact domain's DNS or certificate, an edge, a corporate filter): every server-side instrument reads such an outage as a quiet node. The `artifact_ready` objective holds 99.5% of opens within 3 s. |

## Gauges

A value that goes both ways, sampled at each export.

| Metric | Unit | Attributes | What it makes visible |
|---|---|---|---|
| `crewlet.statelog.drain.rows_per_second` | `1` | `domain` | The applier's observed drain, which every retry hint divides by. Seeded from a benchmark and then measured, so a hint on real hardware stops being an extrapolation from somebody else's. |
| `crewlet.statelog.drain.commits_per_second` | `1` | `domain` | Commits per second, which is the fsync rate under `synchronous = FULL` and the number a device budget is spent by. |
| `crewlet.statelog.apply.lag.seq` | `1` | `domain` | How many records this node is behind the log's head. |
| `crewlet.statelog.apply.lag.seconds` | `s` | `domain` | How OLD the oldest unapplied record is. Seconds are what a stall grace, a pending outcome and a copy taken out of service all turn on; sequences are not, and a lag of 4 000 says nothing about whether anything is wrong. |
| `crewlet.statelog.applied_through` | `1` | `domain` | The prefix this node has actually applied, which is lower than its checkpoint whenever a record was retained. |
| `crewlet.statelog.deferred.count` | `1` | `domain` | Records this build could not read and kept. Non-zero is a rolling upgrade in progress; non-zero and not falling is one that stopped. |
| `crewlet.statelog.deferred.oldest_age_seconds` | `s` | `domain` | How long the oldest retained record has been retained, which is what decides whether this node's copy stays in service. |
| `crewlet.statelog.waiters` | `1` | `domain` | Callers blocked on the applier right now. It is the depth of the queue a slow apply is making. |
| `crewlet.statelog.log.bytes` | `By` | `domain` | What the log actually holds, against its ceiling below. |
| `crewlet.statelog.log.bytes_per_day` | `By/d` | `domain` | What the log took in over the trailing day, measured from its own records at each trim tick. The ceiling has to hold `min_age` of this, because the trim never removes a record younger than that — a log whose ceiling is smaller fills with every trim term satisfied, which is what `log_ceiling_short` fires on. Absent for a compacted log and for one in its first two days, whose trailing day would contain the day it was imported into; a log that could not be read keeps its last measurement, as the report does. |
| `crewlet.statelog.log.max_bytes` | `By` | `domain` | The ceiling, read from the running stream rather than from this node's own configuration — the two differ, and the running one is what refuses the append. |
| `crewlet.statelog.log.headroom_fraction` | `1` | `domain` | How much of the ceiling ordinary writes are held to is left — on every log that claims identity (the tracker, the pages, the identity estate, the artifacts, their datastores and the code log), the ceiling less the gate reserve kept above it for evictions. At zero the log refuses every write AND every linearizable read, and the remedy is a fleet-wide maintenance cycle, so this is the one number worth alarming on long before it is small. |
| `crewlet.statelog.trim.blocked_seconds` | `s` | `domain`, `term` | How long one retention term has held the trim, named. A trim blocked for weeks is a log walking toward its ceiling with a cause an operator can act on. |
| `crewlet.backup.age` | `s` | — | How long ago the newest COMPLETE backup finished, read from the manifests on disk rather than from a counter this process keeps. A counter records that a process believed it took a backup; the disk records that one exists, and they differ in exactly the cases the alarm is for — a copy deleted, a volume never mounted, a schedule pointing at a path nobody ships from. A node holding no manifest reports NO SERIES rather than a value: zero is the freshest backup imaginable and every other number is an age nobody measured, so neither can stand for an absence. The absence is what the `backup_age` alarm says in words, and an `absent()` rule over this gauge is what a collector alerts on. |
| `crewlet.backup.holds` | `1` | — | Live trim holds. A pin that outlives its owner stops the trim until the stale bound expires it, so a count that does not return to zero is a backup that crashed mid-copy. |
| `crewlet.store.wal.bytes` | `By` | `file` | A write-ahead log a checkpoint cannot pass grows, and this is the only way to see it before the volume fills. |
| `crewlet.store.bytes` | `By` | `file` | The store's size on disk, which the snapshot's free-space precondition and the provisioning rule are both derived from. |
| `crewlet.tracker.search.concurrency` | `1` | — | Searches in flight, which is the row of the supported-corpus table this node is actually on: inside the one-second budget, about 345 000 sources with one running and about 136 000 with eight through the full scan, and about 545 000 and 183 000 through an index probing half its lists. |
| `crewlet.tracker.vector.coverage` | `1` | — | The fraction of sources carrying a current vector. It is how a stalled embedding backlog is reported, since it never drops a seat. Absent where the company configures no embeddings and while the corpus cannot be measured — an unreadable corpus is neither covered nor uncovered. |
| `crewlet.objects.s3.gate.limit` | `1` | — | How many attempts this node's S3 client lets its bucket hold at once while a throttle holds it back — seven tenths of the most the node had out at once when the bucket last throttled it, one more each round of answers — and zero while nothing does: the gate lifts a minute after the bucket's last throttle. Above zero for long is a fleet held over the prefix's rate; every request of the node — git syncs, the collector, backups, people's files — shares what it allows. |
| `crewlet.objects.s3.gate.waiting` | `1` | — | Attempts of this node's S3 client waiting in line for the gate, first come first served: what a throttle is costing the node now. High while `crewlet.objects.s3.gate.limit` stays low is a node sending more than the prefix will take from it — its requests wait rather than fail, until their own deadlines. |
| `crewlet.code.compact.behind` | `1` | — | Repositories this node maintains that its last pass found at the most live packs a repository may hold, whose pushes carrying objects are refused `compaction_behind` until a compaction lands: `code_compaction_behind` fires on any. Zero on a node that maintains no such repository. |
| `crewlet.code.cache.bytes` | `By` | — | What this node's git cache holds on disk — every repository's packs, indexes and refs, plus the downloads and pushes in flight — against its byte budget, which it is evicted to, least recently used first, and for no other reason. Sitting at the budget is a cache doing its job; held above it is a repository larger than the budget being served, evicted once nothing reads it; climbing past it while syncs keep starting cold is a budget too small for the repositories this node serves. |
| `crewlet.code.cache.chained` | `1` | — | Repositories this node's git cache serves from an installed published chain — the multi-pack-index layers, each with its bitmap and commit-graph layer, that the repository's maintainer wrote once for every git node and this node fetched and placed — rather than in its own mode, from the index and graph its background work writes itself. Beside `crewlet.code.cache.repos`: the rest are repositories no publication has reached yet, or whose chain this node refused or has not installed (`crewlet.code.cache.layers`). Falling all at once across the fleet, with `layers{outcome=missing}` rising, is an object store that lost the layers' parts — a restore carries none — which every maintainer publishes again; a node serves correctly either way, only slower while it waits. |
| `crewlet.code.cache.maintenance.refused` | `1` | `step` | Repositories this node's git cache cannot write a bitmap (`step` `bitmap`), a commit-graph (`graph`) or, serving from a published chain, its own tip commit-graph over the chain (`tip-graph`) of now, and repositories this node maintains whose next layer it cannot publish (`publish`), because one needs more memory than the node can give its background work — as its latest pass found them. Each refused a bitmap is indexed without one; each refused a commit-graph walks its history by date, so a push of a commit dated before its parent walks every commit; each refused its tip walks the commits pushed since its last publication by date — slower, never refused; each refused its publication serves every pack pushed since its last one outside every bitmap. A bitmap, a graph or a publication above zero raises code_maintenance_refused, since a repository refused its graph is refused its bitmap too; a tip raises nothing, its copy served through its chain's bitmap. Falling back is a repository purged, evicted or rebuilt smaller, a node given more memory, which the cache reads again every ten seconds, or a publication — by this node or by another with the memory, which takes its maintenance over — that its copy installs: its bitmap and graph are then the chain's, and its tail shorter, which lifts a tip refused for its tail's length but never one refused for its repository's size, since a tip keeps room beside its tail for a walking clone of the whole repository. |
| `crewlet.code.cache.memo.bytes` | `By` | — | What this node's git cache holds of answers to seats' reads by object id — a page of a listing, a file, a diff, a comparison — kept so the next read that asks the same is answered from a file rather than from git: part of `crewlet.code.cache.bytes`, each answer counted at the whole disk blocks it takes. Held, with the pages reads are still cutting for it, to a sixteenth of the cache's budget before any repository is evicted — and no repository is evicted for what it holds past that — by dropping the sixteenth of it used least recently at once, so on a node seats read busily it moves between fifteen and sixteen sixteenths of that share, less what is being cut; falling to nothing at once is a history restored or recreated under the node, which drops every answer read from it. |
| `crewlet.code.cache.dropping.bytes` | `By` | — | What this node's git cache holds of packs an expunge's begin has left dropping — what no ref reached when the expunge was planned, kept apart from the live packs so a client still reading one of their objects is served it and no push may rely on one: part of `crewlet.code.cache.bytes`. Zero but while an expunge is open on a repository this node holds; it falls back as each expunge commits and the next sync of the repository takes the dropping packs out. Held up for long is an expunge that began and does not commit — its maintainer's rescue failing — which also refuses every layer the repository would publish meanwhile. |
| `crewlet.code.cache.provenance.behind` | `1` | — | Repositories whose index of which push introduced each commit is behind on this node: a range a full sync passed over that the backfill has not yet read, or a history a seat's reads asked this node, as the repository's home, to read and that it has not yet read to its start. A copy nobody asked about is never read back further than its first full sync, so it is never counted. Until it is zero, an answer naming a commit's push says which range it does not hold rather than answering that no push introduced it. Staying above zero is a backfill that cannot read the data nodes — its warnings, code_cache_backfill_failed, say why — or a history larger than its pace reads in the time it has been asked for. |
| `crewlet.code.cache.repos` | `1` | — | Repositories with a cache on this node. One leaves when its rows are purged or the budget evicts it; every one that arrives cost a cold sync of the whole repository. Falling while the cache's bytes stay at the budget is eviction churn: every repository it drops is a cold sync the next time it is fetched. |
| `crewlet.code.cache.full_rounds` | `1` | `state` | Full reads of a repository's rows this node has against the estate now, by `state`: `running`, each holding one of the node's eight slots from its first page to its last, and `waiting`, in line for one, first come first served. A full read is every repository's first sync after the node starts or joins, a rebuild, every repository's next sync once the code log was recreated or went back under the cache, and a check's or a hint's read of the same rows; a sync after a push reads only what moved and takes no slot. Every page of a full read is one read on a data node — one of the 64 answers its lane gives the whole fleet's reads at once, and one of the reader connections every one of those reads takes, eight on the smallest data node (on a node that holds the data, its own store's) — so the slots keep a node coming up with hundreds of repositories to what the smallest data node scans at once, rather than every page while the fleet's reads wait behind them. `running` at eight while `waiting` climbs is a node bringing up more repositories than it reads at once: each waits inside its own request's time, and they come up eight reads at a time — about four seconds for 500 repositories of a full page of refs each, from a data node of eight cores. |
| `crewlet.code.git.processes` | `1` | `class` | Git processes running on this node, by `class`. `transfer` pinned at `git.max_transfers` while `crewlet.code.git.wait` climbs is a node serving as many clones and pushes as its memory was sized for; `maintenance` is background index rebuilding, at most half of `git.max_processes`. |
| `crewlet.code.git.lent_cores` | `1` | — | Cores of this node's read lane lent right now to pushes as extra index-pack threads — up to three a push, never the last free core. A loan is made when a push's receive-pack starts — the one that receives its pack, never the refs advertisement its first request is answered with — and repaid once its pack is indexed, so it covers the client's whole upload: lent cores held high while `crewlet.code.git.processes` for `read` sits low is slow uploads holding loans, and the reason a later push on this node indexes on one core. |
| `crewlet.code.git.share` | `s` | `share` | What each `share` of this node's transfer lane has spent lately, as the scheduler reads it: core-seconds, every run charged the greater of the CPU it spent and the time it held its slot at the share of a core one slot stands for — the node's cores over its transfer slots, never more than one: a quarter at four slots a core, a whole core where memory or `git.max_transfers` leaves fewer slots than cores — decayed over a minute, the figure the next contended slot is granted by. Set at each admission and release, so a lane idle since holds its last reading. One class's reading far above its weight's share of the total while the others' waits are short is a class alone on the lane, which runs it at full width — `person` and `machine` alike, while `run`, a coding box's, holds at most half of it. |
| `crewlet.code.seatwork.held` | `1` | — | Seat git work running at once on this git node, of half its read lane: the units of the node's seat git-work share held now — server-side reads of a repository by object id running their git, and the builds of engine writes, a seat's or a person's commit made through a tool. The share is half of `git.max_processes` (at least one), and the other half of the read lane stays the node's own and its persons' — a push's scans, a sync's peel, a fetch's check of its wants. Pinned at the share while `crewlet.code.seatwork.waits{outcome=unready}` climbs is a node whose seats ask more git than half its cores, and sends the rest to another git node. |
| `crewlet.alarm.active` | `1` | `kind` | Whether each named alarm is firing right now, 0 or 1 — for one that stands on several logs, whether it stands on any; its `domains` and its log lines say which. It is the same table the operator record renders and the CLI exits non-zero on, so a collector and a person see one answer. |
| `crewlet.objects.bucket.bytes` | `By` | — | How many bytes the fleet's own object bucket on the broker holds (OBJ_crewlet_files: the company's files, their metadata and any upload in flight), as the object collector's duty holder read it; only that node reports it, and only on the nats backend. Read against `crewlet.objects.bucket.max_bytes`: a full bucket refuses every upload, and `objects_bucket_near_ceiling` fires at four fifths. |
| `crewlet.objects.bucket.max_bytes` | `By` | — | The byte reservation the broker holds the object bucket to (store.objects.nats_max_bytes, or the share the node that created the bucket derived): the ceiling the bucket keeps for its life, whatever a node's Tier A says later. |
| `crewlet.artifacts.upload.reserved_bytes` | `By` | — | Bytes the company's upload reservations hold, as this node last wrote the reservation ledger: bytes in the object store, or on their way to it, that no record names yet. Read against `artifacts.limits.pending_bytes` times four, the company's bound: a value that stays near it is clients abandoning uploads, each held until the object collector could have deleted its bytes. |
| `crewlet.artifacts.data.footprint.bytes` | `By` | — | The company's datastore footprint in real bytes held on every data node (each document row with its index and field-index entries, and hot history, as the applier meters what the rows cost on disk), sampled after each committed batch. Read against `artifacts.limits.data_bytes`: a store or a company at its limit refuses every write that grows it. |
| `crewlet.presence.rooms` | `1` | — | Artifact rooms this node holds a member of, a socket's or an agent's. Each costs a map in memory and, while one of this node's sockets is in it, one listen on the broker. |

## Counters

Only ever rises. Rates and totals are your collector's arithmetic, never this engine's.

| Metric | Unit | Attributes | What it makes visible |
|---|---|---|---|
| `crewlet.statelog.publish.outcomes` | `1` | `domain`, `outcome` | The three-valued write outcome, counted, and only the three — a refusal is on `publish.refusals` instead, because it says the write never happened at all. `unknown` is the one that matters most and had no counter: a broker flapping into ambiguity was visible only to the model that received the answer. |
| `crewlet.statelog.publish.conflicts` | `1` | `domain`, `subject_kind` | Writes that spent their whole round budget losing races on one subject, BY KIND. The refusal counter beside it says a conflict happened and not what it was about, and the remedy differs entirely: one contended object is a design question and a contended kind is a hot subject. |
| `crewlet.statelog.publish.rejections` | `1` | `domain`, `subject_kind` | How often a write loses a race, per kind of subject. It is what says whether a counter, a rank order or an ordinary object is the contended one. |
| `crewlet.statelog.publish.refusals` | `1` | `domain`, `reason` | Writes refused before or instead of an append, by `reason`, and EVERY value it carries is here, each with its remedy. The node: `evicted` (this node is removed from the fleet — run the write on another), `eviction_unknown` (its own eviction state could not be read — clears when it is read again), `deferred` (it holds a record it cannot decode — a newer build serves it), `behind` (it has not applied a position the write needs — clears on its own), `below_floor` (it is below the log and must adopt a snapshot — another node writes meanwhile), `floor_unknown` (the domain's floor or the log's ends could not be read — clears when coordination answers, or once a floor row that does not read as its floor is removed). The log: `log_full` (at its ceiling — raise it or unblock the trim), `record_too_large` (the record is larger than the broker takes in one message — split the change; the detail names which limit refused it), `broker_refused` (a refusal this build has no remedy for — the detail carries the broker's own words), `skew` (a store and a stream restored out of step — restore both from one backup), `wrong_stream` (not the log this node's rows came from: rebuilt, ending below its checkpoint, holding another record there, or re-anchored past it by a peer — re-anchor, or adopt where a peer holds the generation), `log_truncated` (it lost records a peer's rows hold — settle which history the fleet keeps). The object: `deleted` (a permanent deletion marker — nothing recreates it). The operation: `op_reused` (its id names a record on another object) and `superseded` (its record landed and a later one undid it) — both answered by a NEW operation under a fresh id, never by a retry. A record that landed and a gate dropped is counted under the gate that dropped it — `evicted`, `deleted`, `abandoned` (written in a generation a reanchor abandoned) or `overtaken` (written after a restored reanchor, below its generation) — and is never re-decided, because republishing makes another record nothing applies. Such a record holds its operation id for the log's duplicate window, so the same id sent inside it, by any node, is collapsed onto the record and refused the same way: the write is retried under a fresh id, or under the same one once the window has passed. Beside the refusals: `conflict` for a write that lost every round, `exists` for a create whose object already exists, and `error` for a write that failed before it could answer. A refusal is not one of the three outcomes: it says the write never happened, and each reason has a different remedy, so one counter with an outcome dimension would hide them all. |
| `crewlet.statelog.read.refusals` | `1` | `domain`, `level`, `code` | Every refusal code, counted. The codes, each with its own remedy, had no counter between them, so an operator had no rejection rate for any of them. |
| `crewlet.statelog.read.served` | `1` | `domain`, `level` | Reads answered per level, which is the denominator every refusal fraction needs and the check on the assumed read rate the log's own size is derived from. |
| `crewlet.statelog.barrier.appends` | `1` | `domain` | Barrier records appended. Against reads served it is the single-flight ratio, which says whether coalescing is doing anything at all. |
| `crewlet.statelog.barrier.applied` | `1` | `domain`, `stream` | Barrier records applied from each log — every node's linearizable reads on it, since every data node applies every record. It is the rate `census_drift` holds against the census, per log: a node's own appends are only its share of the fleet's reads, and on a fleet of several serving nodes they describe a company that many times quieter than it is. The alarm's 24-hour window files each barrier at the hour the broker stored it, so a node replaying a backlog does not read days of reads as one; this cumulative series counts them as they are applied, so it jumps by a backlog's barriers when one is replayed. |
| `crewlet.statelog.linger.yields` | `1` | `domain` | How often a waiter cut a batch short. It is the batching the applier gives up to answer a read promptly, and without it that trade is invisible. |
| `crewlet.statelog.apply.records` | `1` | `domain`, `result` | Records consumed, by what happened to them: applied, retained, gated, skipped, or reprocessed by a build that could read what an earlier one retained — a retained record a gate drops when it is reprocessed is counted `gated`, as it would have been live, since it wrote no row. A node applying nothing while its position advances is healthy on lag alone. |
| `crewlet.statelog.apply.retries` | `1` | `domain` | Attempts the apply loop retried in place after a failure that was not a stop — a fetch the broker did not answer, a transaction the disk refused, an applier that errored. A rate that stays up past the retry budget is a node whose rows have stopped moving, and its health says so. |
| `crewlet.statelog.apply.tx.aborts` | `1` | `domain` | Apply transactions whose body the store ran more than once, because an attempt failed transiently after it began. It reads zero by construction: this database detects write conflicts per file, so every write transaction takes the file's lock at its BEGIN and queues for it, and no commit elsewhere in the file can abort an apply. A non-zero count on the operator's own hardware means the retry budget is being spent rather than held in reserve. |
| `crewlet.statelog.records_gated` | `1` | `gate`, `subject_kind` | Records an apply gate dropped, by the gate that dropped each — the domain's own (`evicted`, `deleted`) or the framework's (`abandoned`, `overtaken`). Each node counts a record once, where its own applier drops it, when the transaction that drops it commits — never once per attempt at that transaction. A write refused because its record — or another node's copy it was collapsed onto — was dropped is a refusal, counted under `crewlet.statelog.publish.refusals`, and not a second drop. A dropped commit is recoverable by nothing, and this is the only place anyone would see that it happened. |
| `crewlet.statelog.records_tampered` | `1` | `domain` | Records whose signature failed under a key this node holds, which means something that is not this fleet wrote to the broker. The applier stops on the first one, so this counts at most one per domain per stop, and any value above zero is an incident rather than a rate. |
| `crewlet.statelog.records_unverifiable` | `1` | `domain` | Records signed under a key this node does not hold, retained until it does. Expected and transient during a keyring rotation; sustained, it means a key reached one node's secrets.keys and not this one's. |
| `crewlet.statelog.anchors.swept` | `1` | `domain` | Arbitration anchors this node's applier removed under the trim's `trimmed` records (ADR-0050), counted once the transaction that removed them commits. Every node applies every record, so every data node counts the same removals. Flat is the normal reading of a log whose purged objects all wrote again later — their anchors moved above the trim and nothing is below it to remove; a sweep that is failing shows as a `retention_anchor_sweep_failed` line from the trim's holder, and as anchors below the log's first record that keep growing while this stays flat. |
| `crewlet.history.answers` | `1` | `question`, `coverage` | What each fleet history read covered: `complete` when every live node answered inside the fleet read budget, `partial` when one did not. Turn-level detail lives only on the node that published it, so a partial answer is missing that node's rows — and the history_partial alarm is a fraction of this counter. |
| `crewlet.tracker.search.answers` | `1` | `coverage`, `semantic` | What each answer actually covered: whether every bucket of the corpus was scanned, and whether the semantic half ran (`full`), was asked for and lost (`skipped`), or was never asked for (`off` — a keyword search, or a company with no embeddings). Both alarms below it are a FRACTION of this counter, and a short answer is indistinguishable from a short corpus without it. |
| `crewlet.tracker.feed.unreadable` | `1` | `source` | Change records this build could not translate into a wake. Both domain consumers are deliberately uncapped, so such a record is never dropped — it redelivers for ever at the head of the consumer with every wake behind it waiting, which has no other symptom at all. |
| `crewlet.tracker.bulk.calls` | `1` | `result` | How often a bulk edit is issued, by `result`: `admitted` under the fleet's bulk lease, `refused` because another is applying, and `fail_open` — let through with NO lease, because the coordination store did not answer the admission or the mixed-version gate refused it. The refusal arithmetic rested on an assumed ten a day, a number with no counter behind it; this is that number. A `fail_open` is a bulk the fleet-wide bound did not cover, and counted as `admitted` it left no trace: a store that refused every admission looked exactly like a fleet whose bulks never collided. |
| `crewlet.tracker.bulk.apply_seconds` | `s` | — | Seconds of applier occupancy bulk edits projected, summed. Over 24 hours it IS the fleet-wide read-degradation budget: every second here is a second in which reads are behind and writes are pending on every node. |
| `crewlet.objects.s3.attempts` | `1` | `operation`, `outcome` | Every attempt this node's S3 client sent its bucket, by S3 `operation` (the API's own name: `HeadObject`, `GetObject`, `PutObject`, `CreateMultipartUpload`, `UploadPart`, `CompleteMultipartUpload`, `AbortMultipartUpload`, `DeleteObject`, `DeleteObjects`, `ListObjectsV2`, `ListMultipartUploads`, and S3 Express's `CreateSession`) and what the bucket made of it (`outcome`): `answered` — served, a success or a refusal such as a missing key; `throttled` — asked to slow down (`503 SlowDown`, any `429`, MinIO's `SlowDownRead` and `SlowDownWrite`), which cuts the node's gate; `failed` — any other answer: a server error that is no throttle, or a status no request expects, such as a redirect to another region; `unreached` — no answer at all: a connection refused or reset, a name that did not resolve, a TLS failure, or an attempt never sent because its S3 Express session could not be had; `stalled` — the bucket stopped moving the attempt for a minute: took no more of its body, acknowledged none of it at the node's socket and sent none of its answer, so the request was given up; `ended` — the attempt's own deadline or its caller ended it in flight. An operation's RETRIES are this counter's total for it, less the count of `crewlet.objects.s3.request.attempts` for it, plus that histogram's `unsent` count for it. `throttled` rising is the fleet over the bucket's rate for the prefix (S3 serves 5 500 reads and 3 500 writes a second a prefix); `failed` the bucket's own fault; `unreached` the network or the endpoint. |
| `crewlet.code.change.proposals` | `1` | `op`, `outcome` | Writes of a change's lifecycle this node's committer was asked to decide, by `op` (`change_open`, `change_edit`, `change_draft`, `change_retarget`, `change_close`, `change_reopen`, and `change_landed`, a landing its repository's home git node found) and what became of each, by `outcome`: `applied`, its record landed and its change's row says so; `unchanged`, it asked for what the change already said, and nothing was appended; `pending` and `unknown`, its record was appended and is not yet known here to have applied; a refusal's own code — `not_permitted`, `stale`, `change_exists`, `no_source`, `no_target`, `same_ref`, `no_difference`, `change_closed`, `change_merged`, `change_not_found`, `repo_archived`, `repo_deleted`, `busy`, `not_applied`, `unavailable` — which decided nothing; `handed_on`, one this node decided nothing of for a reason about itself (stopping, no chart to judge a seat by, behind the company's configuration), which the estate asks the repository's runner-up; and `failed`, any other error. `stale` climbing is askers writing against a change pushes keep moving; `handed_on` on one node and `applied` on another, a node that cannot judge its seats. |
| `crewlet.code.checks.queued` | `1` | `purpose` | Attempts of checks this node's checks writer queued — each a record on its repository's checks subject that applied here, counted once, by the node that published it — by `purpose`: `head`, a change's head; `candidate`, a merge queue's candidate; `tip`, a protected branch's tip; `bisect`, a landing between a green tip and a red one. A head recorded skipped at its dispatch is counted under crewlet.code.checks.finished alone. |
| `crewlet.code.checks.finished` | `1` | `state`, `placement` | Attempts of checks that ended, as their rows keep the ending — counted once, by the node whose checks writer published it — by `state` (`passed`, `failed`, `errored`, `cancelled`, `skipped`) and `placement` (`container`, `e2b`, `external`, or `none` for one no runner claimed). An ending the row did not keep — a later infrastructure ending beside a measurement — is not counted. `errored` climbing on one placement is that placement's cells failing the checks they run. |
| `crewlet.code.checks.claims` | `1` | `outcome` | Claims of queued attempts this node's checks writer decided, by `outcome`: `won`, the claim landed and its runner holds the attempt; `claimed`, refused before it appended — another runner holds the attempt, or it ended; `lost`, the claim landed and the row keeps another runner's, which a second node publishing for the repository landed first; `unchanged`, the holder's own claim sent again; `no_such_check`, `repo_deleted`, `busy`, `not_applied` and `unavailable`, which decided nothing; `pending` and `unknown`, appended and not yet known here to have applied; `handed_on`, one this node decided nothing of for a reason about itself, which the estate asks the repository's runner-up; and `failed`, any other error. `claimed` is git nodes racing for one attempt, each losing one box it never made; `lost` above zero is two nodes publishing one repository's checks at once. |
| `crewlet.code.conversation.writes` | `1` | `op`, `outcome` | Writes of a change's conversation this node's change writer was asked to decide — each a record on the change's own subject, never in the repository's committer queue — by `op` (`reviewers`, `comment`, `thread_resolve`, `review`, `finding_resolve`, and `revise`, a revision's facts its repository's home git node read) and what became of each, by `outcome`: `applied`, its record landed and the change's conversation holds it; `unchanged`, it asked for what the conversation already said, and nothing was appended; `pending` and `unknown`, its record was appended and is not yet known here to have applied; a refusal's own code — `not_permitted`, `no_reviewer`, `too_many_reviewers`, `unknown_revision`, `change_closed`, `change_merged`, `thread_gone`, `not_author`, `not_raiser`, `finding_gone`, `too_many_findings`, `change_not_found`, `repo_archived`, `repo_deleted`, `busy`, `not_applied`, `unavailable`, and a revise's `superseded` — facts of a revision, a head or a target the change has moved from, no later than the facts it holds, or matched against path owners changed since — which decided nothing; `handed_on`, one this node decided nothing of for a reason about itself (stopping, no chart to judge a seat or a reviewer by, behind the company's configuration), which the estate asks the repository's runner-up; and `failed`, any other error. `busy` climbing is a change written faster than one node writes it — its writes wait their turn one at a time — or one the change kept moving under for every round. |
| `crewlet.code.commit.busy` | `1` | `kind`, `reason` | Proposals refused `busy`, undecided, by `kind` and `reason`. `kind`: `push`, whose client runs `git push` again; `compaction`, which the git node that built it plans again at its next pass; `expunge`, a record of an expunge of a repository's unreachable objects — a person's purge request, which they ask for again, or the begin or the commit its maintainer built, which it plans again at its next pass; and `change`, a write of a change's lifecycle, which its asker sends again. `reason` is one of four causes, each pointing at a different remedy. Two are a BACKLOG, which raises `code_commit_busy` on the committer's node: `queue`, a repository taking pushes faster than one node's committer commits them (its queue of 1 024 proposals, or sixteen records' bytes, is full); and `node`, the node holding sixty-four records' bytes of proposals across its repositories. `late` is a DEADLINE, either way round: a proposal that waited behind earlier ones until its asker's attempt had no more left than the 30-second commit budget and a second for the answer, or one that ARRIVED with no more than that left — the attempt spent before it reached the committer, waiting for the node to take it (its proposal slots full), for the node to reach the asker's own writes, or under a caller deadline shorter than 31 seconds; asked with no deadline, one that waited that budget whole. `contended` is a record that lost every compare-and-set round it may take: the repository kept changing, a second committer deciding it during a handoff. Neither of the last two says this committer turns proposals away, so neither raises an alarm. A `compaction` busy is a repository whose pushes keep its committer's queue full, and whose pack count grows meanwhile; an `expunge` busy, one whose unreachable objects stay in the store meanwhile. No repository is an attribute — which one is hot is a question for its rows and the node's `code_commit_busy` lines, a repository a minute, not a time series a repository. |
| `crewlet.code.home.passes` | `1` | `worker`, `outcome` | Turns this node took as the HOME git node of a repository — one worker's work in one repository, scheduled by a nudge from the code log or by the minute's backstop pass — by `worker` (`changes`: its live changes' facts recorded, or a change whose head its target holds landed) and `outcome`: `worked`, its due work done; `failed`, a read or a record that decided nothing for a reason of the node's or the log's (`code_home_turn_failed` says which), the rest worked and the repository listed again by the next pass; and `cut`, more work than one turn's minute, the rest listed again by the next pass. A refusal that the rows moved since — a revision's facts superseded, a landing stale — is the rows answering, and the turn `worked`. `cut` climbing on one node is a home with more changes than its two turns keep up with. |
| `crewlet.code.home.nudges` | `1` | `outcome` | The code log's word to this node's home loop, one a record on a repository's subject, by `outcome`: `scheduled`, this node is the repository's home and its work was queued at the record's position; `elsewhere`, another git node is its home; `unknown`, who serves git could not be read, and the backstop lists the repository within a minute; `ignored`, a subject that names no repository; and `gap`, the watch may have missed records — its consumer lost, its connection back — and a pass was run at once at the position it reaches. Every git node watches every repository, so `elsewhere` is most of every node's count but its homes'; `gap` climbing is a watch that keeps losing its consumer. |
| `crewlet.code.compact.runs` | `1` | `outcome` | Compactions this node made as the MAINTAINER of their repositories — the first git node in each repository's order whose background budget holds its publication, the home on a fleet of alike nodes — each a plan over a repository's live packs that no published layer names, and what became of it, by `outcome`. `applied`: its record landed and its outputs replaced its inputs. `pending`, `unknown`: its record was appended and is not yet known to have applied — the next poll reads the rows. `not_due`: the plan found nothing worth merging, and the repository is not planned again until its row moves. `stale`: another compaction, a publication or a purge moved an input first. `busy`: no maintenance slot or no memory room was free, a publication of the repository was running on the node, or the repository's committer was busy. `refused`: by the committer or before it (`crewlet.code.compact.refusals` says why). `failed`: the build, an upload or the answer failed (`code_compaction_failed` names which). Every outcome but `applied` is tried again at a later poll. `applied` keeping pace with the pushes is a node keeping its repositories' pack counts bounded; `failed` rising is its disk, its git or its object store. |
| `crewlet.code.compact.refusals` | `1` | `reason` | Compactions refused before or at their decide, by `reason`. This node's own: `memory`, the build's charge past what the node can give its background work (`code_cache_compaction_refused` names it, and nothing is built); `store_full`, an object store with no room for an output (the repository is held back until the store shows the room — on a store that reserves nothing, tried again once an hour, as the collector frees room); `outputs`, a build that wrote more packs than one compaction may record, and `bundle_too_large`, an output's bundle past the bound even at a smaller cut — either uploads nothing and halves what the repository's next plan merges. The committer's: `stale`, `busy`, `repo_deleted`, `upload_expired`, `pack_too_large`, `not_applied` and `unavailable`, as for a push. `upload_expired` is a build and its uploads longer than the twelve hours a key may wait to be named, `pack_too_large` the builder's bug: each is logged by name. |
| `crewlet.code.publish.runs` | `1` | `outcome` | Publications this node made as the MAINTAINER of their repositories — each a plan of the repository's next published multi-pack-index layer, its bitmap and its commit-graph layer over every live pack its base does not cover, which every git node installs — and what became of it, by `outcome`. `applied`: its record landed and its layer is the top of the chain. `pending`, `unknown`: its record was appended and is not yet known to have applied. `not_due`: nothing lay outside the chain to publish, and the repository is not planned again until its row moves. `waiting`: a layer of the chain was still at this node's installer, so the plan waited for it rather than replace it. `stale`: another publication, a compaction, an expunge or a purge moved the chain or a pack first. `busy`: no maintenance slot or no memory room was free, a compaction of the repository was running on the node, or its committer was busy. `refused`: by the committer or before it (`crewlet.code.publish.refusals` says why). `failed`: the build, an upload or the answer failed (`code_publication_failed` names which). Every outcome but `applied` is tried again at a later poll; `failed` rising is the node's disk, its git or its object store. |
| `crewlet.code.publish.refusals` | `1` | `reason` | Publications refused before or at their decide, by `reason`. This node's own: `memory`, the build's charge — 900 bytes an object of the repository for the bitmap, with room beside it for a clone — past what the node can give its background work (`code_cache_maintenance_refused` names it with step `publish`, and the repository counts toward code_maintenance_refused for as long; asked again at every pass, and a git node with the memory takes it over); `store_full`, an object store with no room for a part or an output (held back until the store shows the room); `outputs` and `bundle_too_large`, its repack's, as a compaction's; `no_bitmap`, a layer git wrote without a bitmap — no pack it covers holds a commit — even over one more layer; `layer_too_large`, a layer past what sixteen parts of a gibibyte hold. | `crewlet.artifacts.data.writes` | `1` | `verdict` | Datastore writes by verdict. A climb in conflict is people editing the same rows over each other; in forbidden, a page or an agent writing what its collection's rules refuse; in rate_limited, one client spending this node's write budget. |
| `crewlet.presence.frames` | `1` | `direction` | Presence frames this node handled, by `direction`: `client` (a socket's presence frame taken), `peer` (a sealed frame from another node admitted) and `push` (a room's coalesced fan-out to this node's sockets). Presence is told, never stored, so this is the whole of its cost: a `peer` climb with flat `client` is a busy room held on other nodes, and `push` is bounded at five a second per room. |
| `crewlet.objectives.events` | `1` | `objective`, `outcome` | Every service objective's events, by `objective` (the closed set in docs/reference/service-objectives.md) and `outcome` (`good`: answered without fault on the engine's side within the objective's bound; `bad`: anything else). `bad` over all, per objective, against one minus its target is the error budget's burn rate, which the `objective_burn` alarm judges per node over an hour and five minutes and over six hours and thirty minutes; summed across the fleet it is the company's. |

## What is deliberately not here

**Rates.** Every counter is a monotonic total and your collector divides. A
rate computed in this process would be a rate over a window nobody chose,
disagreeing with the one on your dashboard.

**A `/metrics` route.** OTLP reaches Prometheus through the collector you
already run for traces. A second wire format would be a second thing to
authenticate on an API whose guard and whose exemptions are both load-bearing.

**Per-object series.** See the attribute rule above.
